1.pericope_label: Whither is thy beloved gone, O thou fairest among women? whither is thy beloved turned aside? that we may seek him with thee. My beloved is gone down into his garden, to the beds of spices, to feed in the gardens, and to gather lilies. I am my beloved’s, and my beloved is mine: he feedeth among the lilies

schools.summary: Henry makes the enquiry the turning point of the chapter, since the women who had earlier asked what her beloved was more than another are now in love with him themselves; he gives two reasons, that she had shown them his excellencies so that though they have not seen him they believe and therefore love, those who undervalue Christ doing so because they do not know him, and that she had expressed her own love and triumphed in it, so that the flame in her breast scattered sparks into theirs, pious zeal spreading as sinful desire does. He also concedes that, taken as a merely human exchange, an offer to help her seek him would be an indecent compliment, since love is jealous of a rival and would keep the beloved to itself, whereas taken spiritually it is the opposite, those who truly love Christ wanting others to love him too, and the greatest respect the church’s children can show their mother being to join her in seeking him. He keeps the garden enclosed and separated from the world, draws from it the rule that those who would find Christ must attend him in his ordinances, the word, the sacraments and prayer, turns the gathering of lilies toward death, a believer’s death being no more than the owner of a garden plucking a favourite flower which he preserves from withering, and ends where the verse does, that if our own hearts witness that we are his we need not question his being ours, since the covenant never breaks on his side.

Gill notes that the title the companions give her is the one used before, and by Christ before them, repeated to assure her that the question is serious and asked out of respect. On the garden he offers a literal setting first, recalling that the king was said to go out very early in great pomp to a pleasant place some two miles from the city, abounding in gardens and flowing water, or else to the royal gardens below the palace, so that going down is exact; and he then reads the descent as the low estate of God’s people, depressed with sorrows and persecutions, and the condescension of one who visits them there, adding that the church is only recalling what had been said to her already, that he was come into his garden, which she heard and then forgot in sleep. On the mutual claim he holds that her interest in Christ continued through all her unbecoming behaviour toward him, and reports a Jewish commentator who joins the words to the preceding verse so that the sense becomes, though he is gone and I am left alone, I know that I am his and he is mine, a reading he thinks throws a beauty on the words, since the glory of faith is to believe in an unseen Christ, though he allows that she may by then have found him and be speaking as the doubting apostle did.

Clarke assigns the opening question to the bride’s own companions inquiring after the bridegroom, notes that the Hebrew and all the versions join the verse to the preceding chapter rather than beginning a new one, and marks the next verse simply as the answer of the bride to her companions. Wesley allegorizes the answer steadily: the spouse, having sought diligently, at last meets a gracious answer directing her where to find him; the garden is the church at large and the gardens and beds its particular assemblies, in which Christ affords his presence; the spices are the gifts and graces of the Spirit; the feeding is his own refreshment and delight; and the lilies are either individual believers whom he gathers to himself or the prayers and praises of his people in the public congregations.

Keil and Delitzsch supply the setting, since the longing survives her waking as the after-effect of the dream and in the morning she goes out and meets the daughters of Jerusalem, who having made her describe her friend now ask which way he turned, wanting the direction he took so that they may go and seek him with her. They treat her answer as an inference rather than knowledge, since she reasons from the inclination of her beloved to the place where he must be found; and they observe that she never calls him her husband but always her beloved and her friend, love in this song being viewed as far as possible apart from its basis in the animal nature, while the description hovers between the clothed and the unclothed in a way that suits the mystical interpretation.

debates: Why should the companions want to seek him too? Henry answers that jealousy would be natural between human lovers but that those who truly love Christ want others to love him, and traces their change of mind to her description of him and to her own visible joy in him.
Where does the chapter begin? Clarke reports that the Hebrew and all the versions attach this question to the previous chapter rather than opening a new one here.

Does she know where he is? Keil and Delitzsch make her answer an inference from his known inclination rather than knowledge; Gill makes it a recollection of what he had already told her and she had forgotten in sleep; Wesley treats it as a gracious answer given to her diligent seeking.
outliers: Gill recalls that the king was said to go out very early in great pomp to a pleasant place two miles from the city, abounding in gardens and flowing water.
Keil and Delitzsch note that she never calls him her husband but always her beloved and her friend, love here being viewed apart from its basis in the animal nature.
Henry compares a believer’s death to the owner of a garden plucking a favourite flower, which he preserves from withering.
themes: a question asked out of respect
love that wants to be shared
a garden gone down into
faith in an unseen beloved
a covenant that never breaks on his side

4.pericope_label: Thou art beautiful, O my love, as Tirzah, comely as Jerusalem, terrible as an army with banners. Turn away thine eyes from me, for they have overcome me: thy hair is as a flock of goats that appear from Gilead. Thy teeth are as a flock of sheep which go up from the washing, whereof every one beareth twins, and there is not one barren among them

schools.summary: Henry supposes Christ graciously returned to his spouse, having forgiven and forgotten all her unkindness and speaking tenderly to her. He places Tirzah in the tribe of Manasseh and glosses the name as pleasant or acceptable, and dwells rather on Jerusalem, a city compact together which the king had built and beautified, the joy of the whole earth, whose greatest beauty was that it was holy and which prefigured the church. The terror he takes as the church’s own, since censures duly administered strike an awe upon men’s consciences, the word casts down imaginations, and even an unbeliever is convinced and judged by the solemnity of holy ordinances.

Gill hears the speech as a return from silence, the beloved having been absent and silent until now and unable, like another Joseph, to refrain any longer, since for all her behaviour toward him she was his love still. He allows that Tirzah might be the name of some beautiful woman well known at the time, one of the daughters of Zelophehad having borne it, though nothing is said of her beauty, but prefers a city, since the next clause names Jerusalem for the same reason, and this was a place once held by an ancient king of Canaan and later by Jeroboam and some of his successors. On the request to turn away her eyes he will not have dislike in it but the opposite, a man ravished by them and unable to hold out longer, and he reports a rendering that turns the words about, so that she is asked to look him full in the face, having hung her head in shame at their first meeting since her unkindness.

Clarke puts Tirzah in Ephraim and makes it the capital of that district, beautiful in itself and beautifully situated, the residence of Jeroboam before Samaria was built, its name signifying beautiful or delightful, and says the poet compares the bride to the two finest places in the land and the capitals of the two kingdoms. For the army with banners he looks to the caravans of the East, which travel by night divided into companies, each known by the shape of the brazier it carries on a long pole at its head, some holding ten or twelve lights and cut into different forms so that a pilgrim knows his own company by night or day, so that a caravan of many thousands so divided must make a splendid and even a terrible appearance. On the eyes he joins his own image to the sense of dazzling, since after the sight of so many fires the eye cannot bear it, and her look pierced the heart of whoever met it. Wesley takes the whole address as the words of Christ manifesting himself again to his church, makes her terrible to her enemies whom God will certainly destroy, reads the request about her eyes as a poetical way of saying how beautiful she was in his sight, and notes that the lines about her hair and teeth are repeated from an earlier chapter, a repetition he calls not vain but a confirmation that her miscarriage had not alienated Christ’s affection.

Ellicott sees no sufficient reason for naming Tirzah beside Jerusalem except that both were capitals, the one of the northern and the other of the southern kingdom, and takes that to fix the date of the poem within limits; he traces the northern seat of government from the old sanctuary at Shechem to Penuel beyond the Jordan and then to Tirzah, formerly the seat of a petty Canaanite prince, reports two identifications of the site near Mount Ebal, and notes that Tirzah remained the capital only until the reign of Omri. He adds that the Greek and Latin versions render the name by a word for pleasantness, and reports the suggestion that the versions did so to avoid naming the two capitals, since that told against the Solomonic authorship; and he observes that this author is especially fond of comparing his love to familiar places, which was not strange in a language that personified a nation or a city as a maiden. On the verb of the fifth verse he takes the root idea to be showing spirit against oppression, so that the form should mean make me spirited or bold, while granting that the Greek and Latin and many moderns take it as scare or dazzle. Keil and Delitzsch report the inference that the prominence of Tirzah places the Song after the division of the kingdom and its author in the northern kingdom, but hold to the Solomonic authorship themselves and read the verse as the king measuring her beauty by the cities that are the highest ornament of his kingdom; and they derive the verb of the fifth verse from a root meaning to press impetuously against one, taking the intensive form as pressing overpoweringly and infusing a paralyzing terror, with one old version rendering it to put to flight.

debates: When was the poem written? Ellicott takes the pairing of Tirzah with Jerusalem to fix the date after the division of the kingdom; Keil and Delitzsch report the same inference, and the argument that the author was a northerner, but keep the Solomonic authorship; Ellicott adds that the old versions may have dissolved the name into a word for pleasantness precisely to avoid the difficulty.

Where was Tirzah? Clarke puts it in Ephraim, Henry in Manasseh, Ellicott near Mount Ebal on the identifications he reports; Gill will not rule out that the name belonged to a woman rather than a city.

What does the verb of the fifth verse mean? Keil and Delitzsch make it an overpowering assault that infuses terror; Ellicott derives it from showing spirit and would render make me bold, while granting the versions read scare or dazzle; Gill takes the whole request as the language of a man ravished rather than repelled.
outliers: Clarke explains the army with banners from the night caravans of the East, each company known by the shape of the lighted brazier carried at its head.
Henry turns the terror into church discipline, since censures duly administered strike an awe upon the conscience.
Wesley notes that the lines on her hair and teeth are repeated from an earlier chapter, and takes the repetition as proof that her lapse had not altered his affection.
themes: two capitals as a measure of beauty
a name that dates the poem
lights carried at the head of a caravan
eyes that overpower or embolden
praise repeated after a lapse

7.pericope_label: As a piece of a pomegranate are thy temples within thy locks. There are threescore queens, and fourscore concubines, and virgins without number. My dove, my undefiled is but one; she is the only one of her mother, she is the choice one of her that bare her. The daughters saw her, and blessed her; yea, the queens and the concubines, and they praised her. Who is she that looketh forth as the morning, fair as the moon, clear as the sun, and terrible as an army with banners?

schools.summary: Gill takes the repeated descriptions to confirm the reality of the beauty and to show that it continued unchanged despite her failings, and notices that the clause about her lips and speech is left out here, added at the end by the Greek version but absent from the Hebrew copies and unnoticed in the Targum, the Masorah marking some of those words as used only in the earlier place. He defines the three ranks of the court, queens as the principal and lawful wives, concubines as secondary wives admitted to the bed whose children did not inherit, and virgins as unmarried maids of honour in attendance, allows the verse to be read either as an assertion or as a supposition, and cites a Greek poet who gives four times sixty virgins to the wedding of Menelaus and Helena. The oneness he explains two ways, either the small number of the church against the nations and the false churches, like one to sixty or eighty, or her unity as a single body of many members actuated by one Spirit and having one Head, adding that where other princes have many, this one had a single spouse and desired no other. On the closing question he supplies a word of saying to connect it with what precedes, gathers parallels from a Greek poet who gives the dawn rosy fingers, a saffron garment and a golden throne, notes a town named for the splendour of the morning, and turns the gradations of light into the successive ages of the church.

Clarke puts the eighth verse into the bridegroom’s mouth as a concession, that though there be sixty queens and eighty concubines and virgins innumerable, she is the One in whom he delights beyond all; he reports that the queens and concubines, and not the women in general only, praised her as the most accomplished of her sex, and marks the ninth verse as the end of the fourth night of the marriage week. On the closing question he ranks the images by brightness, lovely as the dawn, more resplendent as the moon, and beyond that clear and bright as the sun, yet dangerous to look at and formidable as the lights carried at the head of every company in a great caravan, and adds that comparing a beautiful woman to an unclouded full moon recurs continually in the Asiatic poets. Wesley takes the number as a certain one standing for an uncertain, so that none of the beautiful women in the courts of princes is comparable to her, makes the only one a comparison with an only child, as dear and precious to a parent and especially to a mother as such children are, and assigns the closing question to the queens and concubines wondering how excellent and glorious a person this is.

Ellicott reads the numbers of the court historically and finds them far more sober than those the historical books give, suggesting that the larger figures mark a later form of the traditions about the grand scale on which everything at the court was conducted and that this poetic version is the truer account; he settles the term for maidens as girls rather than virgins from its pairing with the term for concubines. He calls the ninth verse a eulogy on monogamy, which he says was in practice always the rule among the Jews, the exceptions lying only with kings and the very rich, and observes that the praise is sharpened by putting an unconscious testimony to monogamy into the mouths of the queens and concubines themselves. The closing question he assigns to the admiring ladies, argues that the paragraph break belongs at the next verse rather than here, compares the lines in which Juliet is called the sun, and notes that the poet heightens the figure by joining both great lights of heaven to the dawn and putting the praise in the mouths of the lesser beauties of the night. Keil and Delitzsch observe that the same question was asked earlier of the woman being brought to the king, whereas here it is asked of one who moves in what is his as her own, and that the verb of looking forth properly means to bend forward or overhang, since one leans out in order to look.

debates: How many were in the court, and does it matter? Ellicott finds the poem’s numbers far soberer than the historical books and takes the poem for the truer account; Gill treats the figures as an allusion to royal custom or to a wedding procession; Wesley takes them as a certain number standing for an uncertain.

What does it mean that she is but one? Ellicott reads a deliberate eulogy on monogamy, put into the mouths of the rival women; Gill offers either the small number of the true church or her unity as one body; Wesley makes it the affection due to an only child.

Who asks the closing question? Ellicott and Wesley both give it to the admiring women, Ellicott moving the paragraph break to the next verse; Keil and Delitzsch compare the same question asked earlier of a woman being brought to the king, and mark the difference now that she moves in what is his as her own.
outliers: Gill cites a Greek poet who gives four times sixty virgins to the wedding of Menelaus and Helena, and another who gives the dawn rosy fingers, a saffron garment and a golden throne.
Clarke marks the ninth verse as the end of the fourth night of the marriage week, and notes that comparing a beautiful woman to an unclouded full moon recurs continually in the Asiatic poets.
Ellicott compares the lines in which Juliet is called the sun, and hears the praise put into the mouths of the lesser beauties of the night.
themes: a description repeated for confirmation
a court counted three ways
one against sixty and eighty
a eulogy spoken by rivals
dawn, moon and sun in one question

11.pericope_label: I went down into the garden of nuts to see the fruits of the valley, and to see whether the vine flourished, and the pomegranates budded. Or ever I was aware, my soul made me like the chariots of Amminadib. Return, return, O Shulamite; return, return, that we may look upon thee. What will ye see in the Shulamite? As it were the company of two armies

schools.summary: Henry uses the garden verse to explain the withdrawal, since even out of sight he was no further off than the garden, hidden among its trees in a low and dark valley and observing how the vine flourished so that he might do whatever would promote its flourishing; Christ marks the first beginnings of grace in a soul and the early buddings of devout affection, and is as pleased with them as we are with the blossoms of spring. The next verse he gives to Christ as the moment of return, when he could no longer keep at a distance, his repentings kindled together by her lamentation and her languishing desire, so that he resolved at once to fly back.

Gill starts from a custom, that newly married people threw nuts among children for pastime as a sign that they had renounced childish things; he rejects nutmegs, which did not grow in those parts, prefers walnuts, the word being the one the Arabs use, notes that pistachio nuts were well known in the neighbouring country, and reads the nuts as believers, of mean outward appearance but valuable within. On the chariots he allows the words to be either the church’s or Christ’s, since the opening clause may be rendered I know not, and gives two senses on the first reading, that the church, not knowing where he had gone, ran after him as swiftly as those chariots and with a driver’s courage in the field of battle, or that she was in such rapture that she could not tell whether she was in the body or out of it. He derives the name Shulamite from the custom by which a wife took her husband’s name, as a Roman woman was called Caia if the man was Caius, and notes that the root carries both perfection and peace, neither of them hers in herself but both in Christ.

Clarke guesses at the almond rather than the hazel, takes the garden verse and the next to concern the further consummation of the marriage, and cautions that the circumstances of the poem are so interwoven, anticipated and postponed that it is exceedingly difficult to arrange them or to say who is speaking, though other writers find no difficulty because they have a system and the system explains everything. On the chariots he declines the allegory altogether, holding that they were probably proverbial for speed, that the passage marks a strong agitation of mind like what we call palpitation of the heart, and that since he is aware of no spiritual meaning he must be excused from commenting on anything but the letter, adding that the name signifies my princely people though it may equally belong to a man celebrated for his skill in driving. He derives Shulamite as a feminine formed from the king’s name, on the pattern by which Charlotte is formed from Charles or Janette from John, takes the address to be made to her as now the acknowledged wife, and leaves the closing image unsettled, offering the musicians of the camps or the choirs of the bride’s virgins and the bridegroom’s companions while admitting the likeness is not very perceptible, reporting a paraphrase that makes them the camps of two kingdoms, and concluding that the best conjectures afford little satisfaction. Wesley assigns the garden verse to the bridegroom, notes that a valley being low and well watered is fruitful, reads the chariots as a vehement desire for the spouse to be understood figuratively so as to agree with the majesty and omniscience of Christ, supposes the name that of some eminent charioteer known for speed, hears in the fourfold call both a passionate love and her backwardness, and takes the one spouse to be made up of the whole multitude of believers with the two armies confederate, signifying a union of peoples and the strength of a church drawn up like a host.

Keil and Delitzsch keep the scene with the woman rather than the king, since in her loneliness she is happy and finds her delight in moving quietly among growing things, the vine and the pomegranate brought from her home being her favourites; they make her soul, that is her love, the thing that raised her to the royal chariots of her people, where she sits beside the king who drives, and say she knew it and did not know it, being neither elated by it nor ashamed of her origin. The fourfold call they give to the daughters, emboldened by her unassuming answer and entreating her earnestly and even with tears as she walks from the garden to the palace, the verb of looking meaning to sink oneself into a thing by gazing at it; and they note that here for the first time she is addressed by name, which cannot be a pure proper name since the article before it is vocative.

debates: Who speaks the verse about the chariots? Gill allows either the church or Christ, since the clause may be rendered I know not; Henry and Wesley give it to Christ as the moment of his return; Keil and Delitzsch give it to the woman, whose love has raised her to the royal chariots.

How literally should the chapter be read? Clarke takes the garden verses as marriage narrative and refuses to comment on any spiritual sense he cannot see, while noting how hard the poem is to arrange; Gill, Henry and Wesley read the whole allegorically throughout.

What is the company of two armies? Clarke canvasses musicians of the camps, the two bridal choirs and the camps of two kingdoms, and concludes that the best conjectures satisfy little; Wesley makes them confederate armies and a figure of the union of peoples in one church.
outliers: Gill reports that newly married people threw nuts among children for pastime, as a sign that they had renounced childish things.
Clarke admits that the poem’s circumstances are so interwoven and displaced that it is very hard to say who is speaking, and remarks that other writers find no difficulty because they have a system.
Clarke derives Shulamite from the king’s own name, as Charlotte is formed from Charles or Janette from John.
themes: nuts thrown at a wedding
a garden watched from a distance
chariots proverbial for speed
a name taken from a husband
a spouse who is also a host
